refnamediv.refpurpose: The visual properties of the spacecraft

refsection.title: Description
refsection.para: The Spacecraft Visualization Properties lets you define a spacecraft model, translate the spacecraft in X,Y, Z directions or apply a fixed rotation to the attitude orientation of the model. You can also adjust the scale factor of the spacecraft model size. GMAT lets you set orbit colors via the spacecraft visualization properties as well. You can set colors to spacecraft orbital trajectories and any perturbing trajectories that are drawn during iterative processes. See documentation for discussion and examples on how to set orbital colors using Spacecraft object's OrbitColor and TargetColor fields. Also see the section below to read more about these two fields. The Spacecraft visualization properties can be configured either through GMAT’s GUI or the script interface.

Allows you to load a spacecraft's 3D model. The legacy GUI supports .3ds models. The Qt viewer also supports static .pov geometry as described in .

Allows you to set available colors on spacecraft orbits. The spacecraft orbits are drawn using the OrbitView graphics displays. The colors can be identified through a string or an integer array. For example: Setting spacecraft's orbit color to red can be done in following two ways: DefaultSC.OrbitColor = Red or DefaultSC.OrbitColor = [255 0 0]. This field can be modified in the Mission Sequence as well.

listitem.para: Any color available from the Orbit Color Picker in GUI. Valid predefined color name or RGB triplet value between 0 and 255.

entry.para: Allows you to set available colors on a spacecraft's perturbing trajectories during iterative processes such as Differential Correction or Optimization. The perturbing trajectories are drawn through the OrbitView resource. The target color can be identified through a string or an integer array. For example: Setting spacecraft's perturbing trajectories to yellow color can be done in following two ways: DefaultSC.TargetColor = Yellow or DefaultSC.TargetColor = [255 255 0] . This field can be modified in the Mission Sequence as well.

The GUI interface for Spacecraft Visualization Properties is contained on the Visualization tab of the Spacecraft resource. You can configure visualization properties of the spacecraft and visualize the changes in the Display window.

Within the Display window, you can Left click and drag your mouse to change camera orientation. Camera orientation can be changed in Up/Down/Left/Right directions. You can also Right click and drag your mouse to zoom in and out of the Display window. Right click and moving the cursor in Up direction helps to zoom out and moving the cursor in Down direction helps to zoom in.

refsection.title: Configuring Spacecraft Visualization Properties
refsection.para: The legacy GUI supports .3ds spacecraft models. The Qt viewer also supports the static POV geometry described below. Several .3ds spacecraft model formats are available here. You can also download more .3ds models by clicking here. Most of these models are in .3ds format, which can be read by most 3D programs.

refsection.title: Static POV Models in the Qt Viewer
refsection.para: A .pov file describes 3D geometry using POV-Ray's scene language. Select it in ModelFile to use its supported geometry as the spacecraft's visible model. The model offset, rotation and scale settings apply as they do for other spacecraft models.

The Qt importer supports triangle and smooth_triangle surfaces, mesh and mesh2 objects, boxes, spheres, cylinders, cones and tori, unions, solid differences/intersections/merges and declared object instances. It supports scalar/vector expressions, translate/scale/rotate/matrix transforms, solid-color pigments and ambient/diffuse/specular/phong finishes. Include files, scoped declarations and supported string filename expressions can supply shared model data. A mesh2 texture list can select one solid material for a triangle or three materials blended across its corners. Pigment, opacity and the supported finishes use the mission viewer's lighting. Inside a mesh, triangle and smooth_triangle surfaces can also use a texture_list containing three declared texture names, in corner order.

A difference subtracts subsequent solids from its first operand; an intersection retains their common volume, and a merge removes internal surfaces. These operations use the existing display tessellation of closed primitives. Mesh and mesh2 solid operands require a nonzero inside_vector and a closed surface with exactly two faces per matching edge. The importer resolves connected face winding and inside membership before clipping. Inverse complements a supported closed solid. Object transforms, smooth normals and the original corner-material interpolation travel with the clipped surfaces. A completely removed object produces no visible surface.

A torus is centered at the origin about the Y axis and takes major and minor radii. Ring, horn and spindle forms use smooth display tessellation. For a spindle torus, union shows its outer and spindle surfaces and includes the spindle in the solid; merge hides the internal surface; difference excludes the spindle volume; intersection retains only the spindle. The union mode is the default. An intersection mode on a non-spindle torus has no visible surface. Each negative radius toggles inversion, using its magnitude for dimensions. A zero major radius has a spherical boundary; zero minor radius has no visible surface. The optional sturm flag is accepted and has no effect on the viewer's tessellation.

Static numeric expressions support trigonometric and hyperbolic functions and their inverses, square roots, logarithms, exponentials, powers, minimum/maximum, rounding, integer division and remainder, and degree/radian conversion. Vector functions include vdot, vlength, vcross, vnormalize, vrotate and vaxis_rotate. Vector and color components can be selected with .x/.y/.z/.t, .u/.v and .red/.green/.blue/.filter/.transmit. Invalid argument counts, invalid domains and nonfinite numeric results fail with a source location.

Fixed-size arrays support one through five dimensions, nested initializers, indexed reads and assignments, whole-array value copies, #declare/#local scope and element #undef. Elements use the supported numeric, string, object, material, transform or nested-array values. An array's initialized elements share one type; numeric vector widths and material kinds are distinguished. Reading an uninitialized element or using an invalid subscript fails. defined, dimensions and dimension_size inspect declarations and arrays. Indexed values can also supply include filenames. The mixed keyword after array permits different supported value types in different elements and later changes to an element's type. Without it, the shared element type persists even when an element is undefined.

An array declared without dimension brackets is a dynamic, one-dimensional array. It starts empty unless initialized and grows just enough to include an accessed index. Even a defined or #ifdef check grows its nominal size; a missing element remains uninitialized. Fixed arrays retain their bounds. Whole-array copies preserve the dimensions, dynamic or fixed mode, mixed or homogeneous mode, values and uninitialized positions independently.

Prefix an initializer block with optional to allow empty positions or undeclared plain identifiers, for example array[3] optional {1,,3}. Positions still count: fixed arrays require their full positional structure. In a dynamic initializer, a final comma adds no extra element. For multidimensional arrays, place optional on the leaf-row initializer blocks that contain omitted values; the flag does not implicitly pass to nested rows. An uninitialized indexed value still reports its normal read error. Completed rows and values accept the native optional commas.

Parenthesized expressions support numeric/vector and string comparisons, logical !, & and |, and condition ? value : value. Numeric equality and boolean conversion use the default POV epsilon. Both conditional branches and both logical operands are evaluated, as in the native scene parser. select supports its three or four scalar arguments, and strcmp and strlen supply string comparisons and lengths.

Conditional directives #if, #ifdef, #ifndef, #elseif, #else and #end select sections of the model. Inactive sections do not open include files or change declarations. Identifier checks can inspect uninitialized array elements. Control-directive nesting is limited to 200 levels; unmatched or duplicate branches fail with a source location. Message directives report diagnostics, and an active #error aborts the import with its message.

#for and #while can generate repeated model data and geometry. A for loop has a local scalar counter, a bound and an optional step (default one); it supports increasing and decreasing ranges. Bounds and steps are read once. A while loop re-reads its condition after each body pass. Zero-iteration bodies are skipped, and #break exits the nearest loop, switch or macro, including from a nested conditional. Loop-body declarations persist in their normal scopes. A running loop must end in its defining file; its counter must remain scalar and its step must advance it.

#switch reads its scalar selector once. #case uses strict epsilon matching and #range uses inclusive lower and upper bounds. Unmatched clauses are skipped until another label or a default #else. After selection, clauses fall through until #break or #end; later label expressions are still read. A switch must begin with a case or range label and shares the control nesting limit.

#macro defines a named source fragment, with parentheses required for both definitions and calls, including calls without parameters. Each call evaluates its arguments before creating local parameter bindings and executes with access to its caller's scopes. Bare initialized identifiers and array elements refer to caller values; expressions supply private value copies. A local assignment to a reference parameter changes its caller value. Undefining the parameter name removes that local binding; undefining an indexed element clears the actual slot. Optional parameters can be omitted or supplied as uninitialized identifiers; absent parameters create no local binding. Calls must retain the parameter positions, including commas. Definitions are global and can be replaced or undefined. Definitions retain source text without executing their bodies or opening included files. Nested control directives must balance inside the definition. Reaching its end or an applicable #break resumes the caller; call locals then expire.

POV models load in the background in the spacecraft preview and orbit viewer. Changing the selected model or closing its owner cancels the previous import; a completed earlier request cannot replace a newer selection. Canceling the spacecraft model dialog discards its pending validation. Source loops, token scanning, value copies and mesh building check for interruption without imposing an iteration cutoff. A canceled import supplies no partial model. Operating-system file operations and individual library conversions can finish before an interruption is observed. Plot image export asks you to wait while a selected model is loading instead of saving a frame without it.

This is a static geometry import. Dictionaries, infinite CSG operands, open-cylinder/cone CSG operands, cutaway_textures and image/procedural/layered textures are not supported. A closed CSG mesh must use matching edge subdivisions; nonmanifold surfaces and unmatched edges are rejected. An unsupported construct fails the import with its source location; it is not silently omitted from the spacecraft. Camera, light and background scene settings do not replace the mission viewer's controls. Materials use the viewer's lighting rather than a POV-Ray rendered image.

GMAT lets you apply fixed rotation to the attitude orientation of the spacecraft model or translate the model in any of the X, Y and Z directions. You can also apply a scale factor to the selected spacecraft model to adjust the size of the model. Any changes that are made to the spacecraft model, attitude orientation, translation or scale size factor will also be displayed in OrbitView resource’s graphics window. The configured spacecraft visualization properties will only show up in OrbitView graphics window after you have run the mission. See OrbitView resource’s user-specification document to learn more about OrbitView graphics window.
